characters: ONKELOS (day 1): Roman nobleman in his 30s, clean-shaven at first glance but with a short neat dark beard, close-cropped black hair, olive skin, a fine cream wool tunic under a deep purple-bordered cloak, a simple leather belt; calm, amused eyes. ROMAN SOLDIERS (day 1): helmeted legionaries in red tunics and bronze-and-iron armor, short capes, no drawn weapons. THE MAN WALKING HOME (day 2): Jewish man about 45, short greying brown beard, dark wool coat over a white shirt, flat cap; his wife about 40, dark hair under a soft blue headscarf, long navy dress. THE TWO ANGELS (day 2): tall slender figures of soft light, faces gentle and only half-seen, one in warm gold light, one in cool grey-violet light, simple flowing robes, no halos, no wings larger than the shoulders. SHAMMAI (days 3 and 7 memory only): tall, broad-shouldered man about 60, thick dark beard going grey, heavy brows, rough brown builder's tunic, carries a long wooden builder's measuring rod. HILLEL (days 3 and 7 memory only): small, slight man about 70, long soft white beard, kind crinkled eyes, plain undyed off-white wool robe and a simple white head covering. THE STRANGER (day 3): non-Jewish traveler about 30, curly auburn hair, clean-shaven, short green traveling tunic, sandals, a dusty satchel; playful grin. ISRAELITE FAMILY (day 4): mother about 30 in a faded red-brown robe and headcloth, father about 35 with a black beard in a striped tan robe, a girl about 8 and a boy about 5, all barefoot or in rough sandals, carrying cloth-wrapped kneading bowls on their shoulders. MAR SON OF RAVINA (day 5): Babylonian rabbi about 60, long grey-black beard, deep green robe with a white mantle, a tall soft cap; his guests are bearded rabbis in brown, blue and grey robes. JUDITH KAPLAN (day 6): 12-year-old girl, 1922 New York, dark bobbed hair with a white ribbon, a knee-length white cotton dress with a sailor collar, black stockings and shoes, serious and brave. HILLEL'S AND SHAMMAI'S STUDENTS (day 7): young men 18 to 30, Hillel's side in off-white robes, Shammai's side in earthy brown robes, beards of every color, sitting on stone benches. TODAY'S FAMILY (the last picture of every film, always the same people): NOA, 16, long dark curly hair often in a claw clip, gold hoop earrings, oversized cream hoodie or a denim jacket, white sneakers; her brother ELI, 13, short dark wavy hair, a navy knit kippah, braces, a grey crewneck or, on day 6, a slightly too-big navy suit; their MOM, about 45, shoulder-length brown hair, glasses, olive cardigan; their DAD, about 48, short salt-and-pepper beard, black kippah on Friday nights and at shul, blue button-down; SAVTA (grandma), about 75, short silver hair, bright red lipstick, a patterned silk scarf. Warm, modern, ordinary American Jewish family; cool, not corny.

1.story: Onkelos and the mezuzah, Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 11a
1.point: A mezuzah is not a charm: it's a handwritten scroll of the Torah's words (hear, O Israel) on the doorpost, a reminder each time you cross the door of who you are.
1.script: The emperor's own nephew, Onkelos, became a Jew. The emperor was furious. He sent soldiers to bring him back. Onkelos talked with them, and they became Jews too. So the emperor sent more, with one order: don't say a word to him. They marched him out of his house. At the door, Onkelos touched a small case on the doorpost, and smiled. They had to ask: what is that? He said: a king sits inside, guarded from outside. With us, it's the other way around. And they became Jews too. That case is a mezuzah. Inside, no charm. Just handwritten words from the Torah: hear, O Israel. Many Jews touch it on the way out. A reminder of who you are.
pictures: Picture 1: A sunlit Roman villa courtyard, marble columns, a fountain. Onkelos, in his cream tunic and purple-bordered cloak, sits on a stone bench reading an open scroll, a small smile on his face. Behind him, through an archway, a distant red-roofed Roman city. Warm golden afternoon light, painterly, vertical framing with Onkelos in the lower third.

Picture 2: The same courtyard. A small troop of Roman legionaries in red tunics and armor stand around Onkelos, helmets tucked under their arms, listening closely as he talks with open hands. No weapons drawn. Late afternoon light, long shadows, the mood shifting from tense to curious.

Picture 3: Evening. A second, larger troop of soldiers, stern-faced, mouths shut, march Onkelos out of the villa's inner hall toward the front door, one soldier with a hand on his shoulder. Torchlight on stone walls, deep orange and shadow.

Picture 4: Close at the villa's front door. Onkelos, calm, reaches up with two fingers and touches a small slanted wooden case fixed on the right doorpost, and smiles. The soldiers beside him freeze, glancing at each other, curious despite themselves. Warm torchlight on his hand and the case; the night street beyond the door in blue.

Picture 5: An intimate close-up: a scribe's hands at a wooden desk, a goose-feather quill, a small strip of cream parchment covered in neat black ink lines, shown blurred and abstract so no letters are readable, and an open wooden mezuzah case beside it. Soft window light, dust in the air, a quiet sacred feel.

Picture 6: TODAY. Morning in a bright modern apartment hallway in an American city. Noa, 16, in her cream hoodie with her backpack on one shoulder, heads out the front door, touching the mezuzah on the right doorframe with two fingertips and lifting them toward her lips without breaking stride; Eli, 13, behind her tying his sneaker, and Mom with a coffee mug calling something after them. Warm sunlight from the open door, everyday and cool.
motion: Slow push-in toward Onkelos as the fountain water ripples and the scroll edge lifts slightly in a breeze.
Gentle sideways drift across the soldiers' faces as one lowers his shoulders and leans in to listen.
Camera tracks backward ahead of the marching group as torch flames flicker on the walls.
Slow push-in on Onkelos's fingertips meeting the doorpost case, his smile widening slightly, the torch flame flickering.
Very slow tilt down from the quill to the parchment as a fine dust drifts through the window light.
Camera follows Noa from behind as she touches the doorframe and steps into the bright doorway, light flaring softly.

2.story: The two angels who walk you home on Friday night, Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 119b; the two wordings of the Sabbath, Exodus 20:8 and Deuteronomy 5:12
2.point: Shabbat begins at sunset on Friday with two candles, for remember and observe, lit so the family can see each other's faces in peace.
2.script: Friday night. A man walks home from synagogue. The rabbis say two angels walk with him. One good, one bad. At his door, they look inside. If the lamp is lit, the table set, the bed made, the good angel says: may it be like this next week too. And the bad angel has to answer: amen. Even he can't argue with that light. That's why, just before sunset, Shabbat starts with two candles. One for remember the Sabbath, one for observe it. Light first, hands over the eyes, a blessing, then look. A light so the family can see each other's faces. The week stops. Even your phone can wait.
pictures: Picture 1: Dusk in an old stone town, narrow lanes, a deep blue sky with the first star. The man walking home, in his dark wool coat and flat cap, walks alone up a cobbled lane from a small synagogue whose windows glow gold behind him. Painterly, cinematic, vertical, lots of sky.

Picture 2: The same lane, a little further on. Two tall figures of soft light walk on either side of the man, one glowing warm gold, one cool grey-violet, their faces gentle and half-seen; the man doesn't notice them. Their light falls on the cobblestones.

Picture 3: At the man's front door. The man reaches for the handle; the two light-figures stand just behind him, peering over his shoulders through the open door into the house. The doorway glows warmly from inside.

Picture 4: Inside, seen from the doorway: a small warm room with a lamp burning on a white-clothed table set with two braided loaves under a cloth, a cup of wine, and a neatly made bed in an alcove; the wife smiling at the door. The gold angel raises a hand in blessing; the grey-violet angel beside it, reluctant, bows its head as if saying amen. Glowing amber light.

Picture 5: A timeless close-up just before sunset: a woman's hands circling over two freshly lit white candles in silver candlesticks, then covering her eyes; the window behind her shows an orange sunset. Soft, quiet, sacred.

Picture 6: TODAY. Friday night in a warm modern dining room. Mom has just uncovered her eyes in front of two lit candles; Dad in his black kippah, Savta in her silk scarf, Noa and Eli around the table laughing, a challah under an embroidered cloth, and two phones lying face down on a side shelf. Golden candlelight on every face, cozy and real.
motion: Slow crane up from the man's footsteps to the first star as the synagogue windows glow behind him.
Camera drifts alongside the three figures as the angels' light gently pulses on the stones.
Slow push over the man's shoulder through the opening door into the warm room.
Gentle push-in on the lit lamp as the flame sways and the grey angel's head slowly bows.
Close hold as the hands circle the flames twice and come to rest over the eyes, candle flames flickering.
Slow orbit around the table as the candle flames flicker and the family laughs.

3.story: Hillel and the man on one foot, Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a; Hillel's saying in Mishnah Avot 2:5
3.point: A mensch, the Yiddish word for a real human being, is someone decent when nobody's checking, which is what Hillel taught: don't do to others what's hateful to you, and where no one acts humanely, be the one who does.
3.script: A stranger walked up to the great teacher Shammai with a dare. Teach me the whole Torah while I stand on one foot. Shammai, a builder, chased him off with his measuring stick. So the stranger tried another teacher, Hillel. Same dare. Hillel didn't flinch. What's hateful to you, don't do to anyone else. That's the whole Torah. The rest is explanation. Now go and learn it. Hillel also taught: where nobody is acting like a real human being, try to be one. Yiddish gave that a single word. Mensch. Not a genius. Not a saint. Just decent, when nobody's checking. When the group chat piles on someone, be the mensch.

open.text: a teacher chased him off with a *stick*.

pictures: Picture 1: A busy stone courtyard in ancient Jerusalem, morning light. The stranger, in his green traveling tunic with his dusty satchel, stands balanced on one foot with arms out, grinning, in front of Shammai, who stands holding his long wooden measuring rod beside a half-built stone wall. Onlookers watch from the edges.

Picture 2: The same courtyard, a moment later, comic not violent: Shammai, frowning under heavy brows, waves his measuring rod in the air; the stranger hops backward on one foot, laughing, scrambling away. Dust kicked up, bright midday light.

Picture 3: A quiet, shaded doorway of a modest house. The stranger, still a little dusty, knocks; Hillel, small and white-bearded in his off-white robe, opens the door with a warm, curious look. Vines on the wall, soft afternoon light.

Picture 4: Inside a simple room. The stranger stands on one foot again, wobbling; Hillel, seated on a low stool, gently raises one finger as he speaks, smiling. The stranger's face changes from cheeky to stunned. Warm lamplight, intimate framing.

Picture 5: A wide, golden view of Hillel seated on stone steps in the evening, surrounded by a circle of listeners of different ages, the former stranger among them now listening intently. Long shadows, a sense of something passed on.

Picture 6: TODAY. A school hallway at the lockers. Noa, 16, in her denim jacket, has stepped in beside a younger kid who is alone, holding up her phone to show him something and laughing with him, while two other students nearby look at a screen and smirk. Eli, 13, in his grey crewneck and navy kippah, walks over to join them. Bright daylight from tall windows, natural, kind.

Quick but gentle sideways pan following the stranger hopping away as Shammai's rod swings.
Slow push toward the doorway as it opens and warm light spills out across the stranger.
Gentle push-in on the stranger's face as his grin fades to wonder and the lamp flickers.
Slow pull-back revealing the whole circle of listeners as the evening light deepens.
Handheld-style drift down the hallway toward Noa and the kid as Eli steps into frame.

4.story: The night of leaving Egypt, Exodus 12:31-39; the seder's answer, Mishnah Pesachim 10:4-5 and the Haggadah ('we were slaves')
4.point: The seder retells the Exodus with matzah, the bread that had no time to rise, and its answer starts with 'we were slaves', because every generation tells it as their own story.
4.script: Egypt. Midnight. After ten plagues, the king finally gives in: get out. Now. A whole people of slaves, and no time. The bread dough hadn't risen yet. So they wrapped it, still in the bowls, in their cloaks, threw it over their shoulders, and walked out into the dark. On the road, they baked it flat. Matzah. Ever since, on Passover night, families eat that bread. At the seder, the youngest asks: why is this night different from all other nights? And the answer doesn't start with once upon a time. It starts with: we were slaves. We. In every generation, each person should see themselves as if they walked out of Egypt. It's not their story. It's yours.

open.text: they left before the bread could *rise*.

pictures: Picture 1: Midnight in ancient Egypt. A wide view over a mud-brick slave village beside a river, palm trees and a distant stone temple under a huge moon; families stream out of their doorways with bundles and lamps, a sense of sudden urgency. Deep blue night with warm lamp-glow. No violence, no bodies.

Picture 2: Inside a small mud-brick home lit by one oil lamp. The Israelite mother lifts a wooden kneading bowl of pale, flat, unrisen dough; the father ties a cloak around another bowl; the girl and boy watch, wide-eyed. Hurried, intimate, warm shadows.

Picture 3: A vast crowd of people walking out across the desert at night under the stars, seen from behind, carrying cloth-wrapped kneading bowls on their shoulders, children holding hands, animals among them. The Israelite family in the foreground. A distant leader far ahead is only a small silhouette seen from behind. Silver moonlight on sand.

Picture 4: Dawn on the road. The Israelite family kneels by a small fire on a flat hot stone, the mother laying out thin flat rounds of dough to bake; smoke curls up into a pink-orange sky. Desert hills behind.

Picture 5: A candlelit seder long ago, in a wood-paneled old European home: a long table with a white cloth, a seder plate with a roasted bone, an egg, parsley, horseradish and a brown sweet paste, a stack of matzah, cups of wine; the youngest child stands on a chair, asking, while the family watches with smiles. Any books on the table show only blurred, unreadable pages.

Picture 6: TODAY. A crowded, happy modern seder in a family dining room with borrowed folding chairs. Dad in his kippah reads from a Haggadah, Savta points at the seder plate, Noa, 16, leans in laughing, and Eli, 13, holds up a piece of matzah; younger cousins around the table. Warm lamplight, wine cups, real and lively. Book pages blurred, no readable text.

Slight push-in as the mother lifts the dough bowl and the lamp flame wavers.
Slow aerial drift forward over the walking crowd as cloaks flutter in the night wind.
Gentle push-in on the flat dough on the hot stone as smoke curls upward into the dawn.
Slow dolly along the table toward the child standing on the chair as the candles flicker.
Gentle orbit around the modern table as Eli lifts the matzah and everyone laughs.

5.story: Mar son of Ravina breaks a precious cup at his son's wedding feast, Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 30b-31a; remembering Jerusalem, Psalms 137:5-6
5.point: A glass is broken at the end of a Jewish wedding so that even at the height of joy we remember what is still broken, starting with Jerusalem, and then everyone shouts mazel tov.
5.script: Ancient Babylon. A wedding feast. A great rabbi, Mar son of Ravina, is marrying off his son. The wine is flowing. The rabbis at the tables are getting louder. And louder. So he brings out his most precious cup, worth a fortune, and smashes it, right in front of them. Silence. Everyone sobers up. Later teachers kept the crash, and gave it a reason: Jerusalem, and its Temple, destroyed. Even at your happiest, remember what's still broken. That's why a Jewish wedding ends with a glass, wrapped in cloth, crushed underfoot. Then everyone shouts mazel tov. On your best day, you can still remember who isn't there.

open.text: a rabbi smashed his best cup *on purpose*.

pictures: Picture 1: A grand courtyard in ancient Babylon at night, hung with lanterns and woven rugs, long low tables of food and fruit, palm trees, a starry sky. Mar son of Ravina, in his green robe, white mantle and tall cap, stands proudly at the head of the feast. Rich warm gold and deep teal.

Picture 2: The same feast, closer. Bearded rabbis in brown, blue and grey robes laugh loudly, raise cups, one standing on a cushion telling a story, cups tipping; the party getting out of hand in a cheerful way. Lantern light swinging, lively.

Picture 3: Mar son of Ravina lifts a gleaming, jeweled crystal-and-gold cup high above his head with both hands, his face serious, in front of the startled guests. The cup catches the lantern light. The moment just before it falls.

Picture 4: Silence. Glittering fragments of the cup scattered across a woven rug in the lantern light; the guests frozen, cups lowered, faces suddenly sober. A hush, deep shadows, one lantern swaying. No injury.

Picture 5: A wide, quiet dusk view of Jerusalem's ancient stone walls and the great stones of the Western Wall, warm last light on the stones, a few birds, a sense of longing. No people, no fire, no ruins smoking.

Picture 6: TODAY. A modern Jewish wedding under a flower-covered chuppah outdoors at golden hour. Seen from among the guests: a foot in a polished shoe coming down on a glass wrapped in white cloth, and all around, the guests mid-shout with joy, arms in the air. Noa, 16, and Eli, 13, in the front row cheering, Savta clapping, Mom and Dad laughing. Focus on the family and the crowd, not on the couple.
motion: Slow push-in across the feast toward Mar son of Ravina as lanterns sway in a light wind.
Gentle sideways drift along the rowdy table as cups lift and lantern light swings.
Slow push-in up toward the raised cup as it gleams, the guests' faces turning upward.
Very slow pull-back from the glittering fragments as the swaying lantern settles still.
Slow pan across the ancient stones as the dusk light fades and birds cross the sky.
Quick small push-in as the foot comes down, then the crowd erupts and arms fly up.

6.story: Judith Kaplan's bat mitzvah, the first public bat mitzvah in America, New York, 18 March 1922; the ages of the commandments, Mishnah Avot 5:21 and Talmud Niddah 45b
6.point: You don't 'have' a bar or bat mitzvah, you become one: at twelve or thirteen the mitzvot, the commandments, become your own responsibility, and the ceremony just says it out loud.
6.script: New York, 1922. A Saturday morning. A twelve-year-old girl, Judith Kaplan, stands in front of her father's congregation. She says the blessings and reads from the Torah, out loud, from a printed book. A girl. In public. Almost nobody had ever seen that. It's remembered as the first public bat mitzvah in America. But here's the twist. By Jewish law, she was already bat mitzvah, the day she turned twelve. Boys, at thirteen. It comes on its own. Bat mitzvah: daughter of the commandment. Mitzvah: what the Torah asks of you. The ceremony just says it out loud. Until then, your choices were your parents' to answer for. Now, they're yours.
pictures: Picture 1: A New York street in March 1922, early morning: brownstones, a Model T, people in long wool coats and hats walking toward a modest synagogue entrance; Judith Kaplan, in her white sailor-collar dress under a dark coat, walks with her hand in her father's (seen from behind, in a dark suit and hat). Soft grey-gold morning light.

Picture 2: Inside a simple 1920s synagogue with wooden pews and tall windows. Judith stands at the front, small and brave, reading aloud from an open printed book on a lectern; the congregation, men and women in 1920s clothes, watch. Pages blurred, no readable text. Warm window light falling on her.

Picture 3: The congregation's faces seen from Judith's side: some surprised, some smiling, an older woman with a hand over her heart, a boy leaning forward to see. Painterly, warm, a feeling that something new just happened.

Picture 4: A small 1920s family kitchen, an ordinary weekday months earlier: Judith blowing out twelve candles on a simple cake while her mother smiles, nothing grand about it. Morning light through lace curtains.

Picture 5: A close-up of an open Torah scroll on a velvet-covered reading table, a silver pointer (yad) resting on it, the columns of writing shown soft and blurred so nothing is readable. A beam of light falls across it. Quiet and sacred.

Picture 6: TODAY. A modern living room the evening before Eli's bar mitzvah. Eli, 13, in his slightly too-big navy suit jacket over a T-shirt, practices from a booklet; Noa, 16, sits on the arm of the couch coaching him and laughing; Mom, Dad and Savta watch from the kitchen doorway, proud. Warm lamp light, pages blurred, real and funny.
motion: Slow tracking shot following Judith and her father up the sidewalk as steam rises from a street grate.
Slow push-in toward Judith at the lectern as dust floats in the window light.
Gentle pan across the congregation's faces as the older woman presses her hand to her heart.
Close hold as Judith blows and the twelve small flames bend and go out.
Very slow tilt along the scroll to the silver pointer as the light beam brightens.
Gentle push-in on Eli as Noa gestures and he grins, the family blurred in the doorway.

7.story: These and these are the words of the living God: the schools of Hillel and Shammai, Babylonian Talmud, Eruvin 13b; an argument for the sake of heaven, Mishnah Avot 5:17
7.point: Machloket, disagreement, is how Jewish learning works: an argument for the sake of heaven keeps both sides, and the law followed Hillel because his students were humble and taught the other side first.
7.script: Two schools of rabbis, in the land of Israel, two thousand years ago. Hillel's students, and Shammai's. For three years they argued. How to live, how to pray, what the Torah really asks. Each side said: the law follows us. Then, the Talmud says, a voice came from heaven. These and these are the words of the living God. Both. But the law follows Hillel. Why? Because Hillel's students were kind and humble. They taught the other side's view along with their own, and even taught it first. That's machloket: an argument for the sake of heaven, with the losing side written down and kept. Next time you argue, say their side first. Fairly. Then yours.
pictures: Picture 1: A great stone study hall in the ancient land of Israel, arched windows, oil lamps, scrolls in niches. Two groups of young students sit on facing stone benches: Hillel's in off-white robes on the left, Shammai's in earthy brown robes on the right. Warm afternoon light in a wide, vertical composition.

Picture 2: The same hall, mid-argument: students from both sides leaning forward, hands raised, one standing and pointing at an open scroll (writing blurred), another counting points on his fingers; passionate but not angry. Seasons passing are hinted at through the windows: a leafless tree on one side, a blooming one on the other.

Picture 3: A sudden hush in the hall. A soft, wide beam of golden light pours down through a high window onto the space between the two groups, and every student looks up, startled and awed. No figure, no face, only light and dust in the air.

Picture 4: Hillel's students, in their off-white robes, bend over a scroll together with two of Shammai's students in brown, one of Hillel's students carefully pointing at the Shammai students' lines first while they nod in surprise. Gentle lamplight, humble and warm.

Picture 5: A close-up of an old bound Talmud-style page layout shown as soft abstract blocks of blurred ink, a central column surrounded by commentary columns, on a wooden study table with two cups of tea and two pairs of hands pointing at different blocks. No readable text. Warm lamplight.

Picture 6: TODAY. A cozy kitchen table at night. Noa, 16, and Dad sit across from each other with an open book between them (pages blurred), mid-debate and both grinning, Noa counting a point on her fingers, Dad raising his eyebrows; Eli, 13, eats cereal and watches like it's a sports game; Savta laughs in the background. Warm overhead light, lively and real.
motion: Slow push-in down the aisle between the two benches as lamp flames flicker.
Gentle sideways drift across the arguing students as hands rise and the light through the windows shifts.
Slow crane up along the beam of light as dust sparkles and the students' faces lift.
Slow push-in on the shared scroll as the pointing hand moves and the others nod.
Very slow top-down drift over the page blocks as the tea steams.
Gentle back-and-forth push between Noa and Dad as they gesture and Eli looks from one to the other.

sources_check: Day 1: Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 11a (Onkelos and the mezuzah); Gittin 56b (Onkelos as the son of Titus's sister); Deuteronomy 6:4-9; Maimonides, Laws of Mezuzah 5:4 (not an amulet)
Day 2: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 119b (the two ministering angels and the lit lamp); Exodus 20:8 and Deuteronomy 5:12 (remember, observe); Shabbat 23b (the Shabbat light for peace in the home)
Day 3: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a (Shammai's builder's cubit, Hillel's 'what is hateful to you'); Mishnah Avot 2:5 (where there are no men, strive to be a man)
Day 4: Exodus 12:31-39 (Pharaoh's 'get out', the kneading bowls bound in their cloaks, unleavened cakes baked on the way); Mishnah Pesachim 10:4-5; the Haggadah (the four questions; avadim hayinu)

Day 5: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 30b-31a (Mar son of Ravina breaks a cup worth 400 zuz at his son's wedding); Psalms 137:5-6; Tosafot to Berakhot 31a and Rema, Orach Chaim 560:2 (the glass and remembering Jerusalem)

Day 6: Judith Kaplan Eisenstein's bat mitzvah, 18 March 1922, Society for the Advancement of Judaism (Jewish Women's Archive); Mishnah Avot 5:21; Babylonian Talmud, Niddah 45b (twelve for a girl, thirteen for a boy); Genesis Rabbah 63:10

Day 7: Babylonian Talmud, Eruvin 13b (three years of dispute, the heavenly voice, why the law follows Beit Hillel); Mishnah Avot 5:17 (an argument for the sake of heaven); Mishnah Eduyot 1:5-6 (minority views recorded)
risks: Day 1: The Talmud tells of three troops of soldiers (the first two converted after Onkelos spoke with them, the third was told not to speak with him and converted at the mezuzah); the film compresses the second and third into 'the emperor sent more'. Calling him the emperor's nephew draws on Gittin 56b (son of Titus's sister); Avodah Zarah 11a just says 'the emperor'. Onkelos's line implies God guards the house, which sits alongside the lesson's 'not a charm' framing; a scholar should confirm the balance reads right.

Day 2: Shabbat 119b says the angels find 'a lamp lit, a table set, a couch spread'; the film says 'lamp' and 'bed made', then moves to the custom of two candles. The angels are depicted as figures of light; check that this suits the audience and that it's clear this is a rabbinic story, not Torah.

Day 3: Hillel's answer is paraphrased ('the rest is explanation' for 'the rest is commentary'). Shammai is shown waving his measuring rod comically; the Talmud says he pushed the man away with it. Make sure Shammai isn't painted as a villain, since day 7 honors both schools.

Day 4: 'After ten plagues' and 'the king finally gives in: get out' follow Exodus 12:31; the plagues aren't shown. Moses is only a distant silhouette from behind. The baking 'on the road' follows Exodus 12:39.

Day 5: The link from Mar son of Ravina's cup to today's wedding glass and to Jerusalem comes from later commentators (Tosafot, the Rema), not the Talmud itself; historians debate the custom's origins. 'The wine is flowing' fairly glosses the Talmud's 'the rabbis were very merry'.

Day 6: Judith Kaplan read from a printed Chumash, not from the Torah scroll; the script says 'from a printed book' but picture 5 shows a scroll as a symbol, which should not be read as what she used. 'First public bat mitzvah in America' is the usual claim (Jewish Women's Archive). Communities differ on bat mitzvah age and on what women do in the ceremony; the script states only the traditional legal ages and stays neutral.

Day 7: The heavenly voice's words are a quote from Eruvin 13b ('these and these are the words of the living God'), not invented; the voice is shown only as light. Where the two schools sat (Jerusalem or elsewhere) is not certain, so the script says 'the land of Israel'.
